newsitem.title: USA: Stocks roar back after shaking off Greenspan effect.
newsitem.headline: Stocks roar back after shaking off Greenspan effect.

text.p: Stocks jumped Monday and the Nasdaq index rallied to a record close in a sharp turnaround from Friday's sell-off sparked by comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that rattled markets around the world.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 82.00 points at 6,463.94, its biggest point gain since a 97-point rise on Nov. 6 in a post-election euphoria.
The Nasdaq Composite index set a record, gaining 28.59 points 1,316.27, surpassing the old record of 1,300.37 set on Dec. 3.

On Friday, the Dow lost 55 points after Greenspan's warning about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets was viewed as a hint that the central bank might resort to higher interest rates to slow the ascent of financial markets.
At one time Friday, the world's most closely watched stock index tumbled nearly 145 points -- its steepest drop since July 15 when it tumbled 161.05 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,919 to 632 on heavy volume of 381 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The underlying fundamental is that Greenspan is not in a position to raise rates," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.

Investors sensed that they had overreacted to the Fed chief's comments, which were made in a speech delivered Thursday night, and there was a consensus that Greenspan would have a tough time justifying an interest rate increase as the economy slowed.

"I think Greenspan is saying he wants us to be cautious, not comfortable about where the market is right now. Cautious does not mean bearish," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"What we're seeing in the Dow and S&P 500 is a continuation of the snapback we saw Friday," he said.
The bond market also bounced back, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury up more than half a point to send its yield down to 6.47 percent from 6.54 percent at Friday's close.
Big-name high technology stocks lured strong buying.

International Business Machines surged 4-3/8 to 160 and Microsoft jumped 5-3/8 to 81-3/4 in its first day of trading after a two-for-one stock split. Intel climbed 4-7/16 to 130-1/8 and Cypress Semiconductor added 1-5/8 to 15-1/2.
Among individual stocks, Dow component Philip Morris rallied 4-3/4 to 114-1/4 after Goldman Sachs raised its 12-month price target for the company to $135 from $125.

Santa Fe Pacific Gold rose 1-1/4 to 16-1/2 after Homestake Mining emerged as a so-called "white knight" bidder with a buyout offer of $17.42 a share, or $2.3 billion. The bid followed Newmont Mining's proposal last Thursday to acquire Santa Fe for $2 billion in stock. Homestake fell 7/8 to 14-3/4 and Newmont Mining rose 1/8 to 47.
British Airways rose 3-7/8 to 99-1/4 in U.S. trading on signs Britain would approve an alliance with American Airlines. AMR Corp., the parent of American Airlines added 2-1/4 to 91-3/4.

Centennial Technologies rallied 5 to 46-1/4 on news that it acquired a 12 percent stake in ViA Inc. for undisclosed terms. ViA is a privately held technology company that makes miniature communication and computing products.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 10.16 to 749.76. The American Stock Exchange index rose 4.78 to 590.48.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 4.54 to 394.69. The average share was up 47 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,2637.93 up 95.349 or 1.33 percent.
